title: The pure spring
hookLine: curse a clear spring and it keeps flowing clear (Meditations 8.51)

lines: WATER YOU CAN COUNT PEBBLES IN.
cards: A spring in the hills, the water so clear you can count the pebbles. Someone stands at the edge and shouts at it. Calls it names.
Kicks dirt into it. What does the spring do? Nothing dramatic.
It keeps coming up from below, and in a minute the water's clear again. Marcus put that picture in book eight, right after imagining the worst that people could do to him.

teach.b: The entry starts bluntly: suppose people kill you, cut you to pieces, curse you. What can any of that do to stop your mind from staying pure, wise, sober and just? He isn't saying it wouldn't hurt.
He's asking what it can reach. Then the spring. Imagine, he says, someone standing beside a clear, sweet spring and cursing it.
The spring doesn't stop sending up good water. Throw in mud, or worse, and it quickly scatters it, washes it out, and isn't stained.
It isn't defending itself; it's still flowing from below, faster than the dirt can settle.

teach.h: CURSE A SPRING; IT KEEPS FLOWING.
teach.b: So how, Marcus asks, can you have an ever-flowing spring inside you, and not just a well, a still pit that holds whatever is thrown in?
His answer: keep shaping yourself, hour by hour, toward freedom, with kindness, simplicity and modesty.
A well depends on what reaches it. A spring has its own source. This isn't pretending an insult didn't land.

teach.h: CLOUDY FOR A MOMENT, THEN CLEAR.
teach.b: Even a clear spring goes cloudy for a moment. The point is what happens next: whether the mud sinks in and stays, or gets carried off by what keeps rising.
Earlier in the same entry Marcus gives himself a short list: don't be sluggish in action, or muddled in conversation, or wandering in thought.
The spring is that list, kept running.

how: Readers of Marcus often use the spring as a picture after an insult: they let the sting register, then turn their attention back to what they meant to do anyway, and let the words settle and wash out.

o: a decorative water jet in a town square
a spring that keeps rising and washes dirt away
a still well that holds whatever falls into it

games.q: the pure spring — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus says an insult shouldn't hurt at all
he asks what it can reach, not whether it stings; even a clear spring goes cloudy for a moment.
in Marcus's image, dirt thrown into the spring is quickly scattered and washed out
the spring keeps sending up clean water, and isn't stained.

games.q: you're the spring. someone stands at the edge, cursing you and kicking dirt in. what do you do?
o: keep flowing, and let the water carry the dirt away.
flood the bank to drive them off.
games.why: Marcus says the spring never stops sending up good water, and quickly washes out what's thrown in, without being stained.

practice: Bring to mind one sharp thing someone said to you recently, something small, and notice where it lands: chest, jaw, stomach. Picture the words falling into the spring like a handful of dirt, and don't push them out.
Feel what keeps rising underneath, your breath, your steadiness, the good you meant to do today anyway, and watch the water clear, a little at a time.

wordCard.voice: Fountain. Marcus's picture: curse a clear spring, throw dirt in it, and it keeps sending up clean water that carries the dirt away. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a spring, a fountain, water rising from its own source.

carryVoice: Your line: the spring runs clear. Cloudy for a moment, then clear again, carried by what rises. Until tomorrow.
